questions.prompt: Explain three differences between a typical photosynthetic plant cell and a bacterial cell.
scheme: 1 · Plant DNA is enclosed in a nucleus; bacterial DNA is not.
2 · The plant cell has chloroplasts; the bacterium does not.
3 · The plant cell has a permanent vacuole; the bacterium does not.

questions.prompt: A cell is 50 μm across. A bacterium is 0.5 μm across. Calculate how many orders of magnitude larger the cell is.
scheme: 2 · 100 = 10², so two orders of magnitude.

questions.prompt: Describe the functions of four structures found in a palisade leaf cell.
scheme: 1 · Nucleus contains genetic material that controls the cell.
2 · Chloroplasts absorb light for photosynthesis.
3 · Cellulose cell wall strengthens/supports the cell.
4 · Permanent vacuole contains cell sap / keeps the cell turgid. Accept mitochondria for respiration, ribosomes for protein synthesis, membrane controls movement of substances.

questions.prompt: Which structure makes proteins?
scheme: Ribosome

questions.prompt: Where is the main bacterial DNA?
scheme: Free in cytoplasm

questions.prompt: Which structure is found in plant cells but not in animal cells?
scheme: Plant cells have cellulose cell walls; animal cells do not.

questions.prompt: What is a plasmid?
options: A small ring of DNA in a bacterium
scheme: Plasmids are small extra rings of DNA found in many bacteria.

questions.prompt: Bacteria are described as prokaryotic because…
options: their genetic material is not in a nucleus
scheme: Prokaryotic cells have no nucleus.

questions.prompt: Which organelle releases most of the energy from aerobic respiration?
scheme: Aerobic respiration takes place mainly in mitochondria.

questions.prompt: A cell image is 54 mm wide at ×1800. Calculate actual width in micrometres.
scheme: 1 · Actual size = image size / magnification.

questions.prompt: A student draws a cheek cell 60 mm wide. The real cell is 60 μm wide. Calculate the magnification of the drawing.
Compare light microscopes and electron microscopes. Explain how electron microscopy has improved our understanding of cells.
scheme: 1 · Electron microscopes have higher magnification.
2 · Electron microscopes have higher resolution / can distinguish two points closer together.
3 · So smaller subcellular structures (e.g. ribosomes, internal structure of mitochondria/chloroplasts) can be seen.
4 · Light microscopes are cheaper/portable and can view living specimens in colour.

questions.prompt: A 20 μm cell appears 40 mm long. Calculate magnification.
What distinguishes two close organelles?
scheme: High resolution

questions.prompt: An image is 12 mm long. The real object is 0.03 mm long. What is the magnification?
How many micrometres are in 1 mm?
Which of these can only be seen clearly with an electron microscope?
scheme: Ribosomes are too small to resolve with a light microscope.

questions.prompt: Write 0.000 005 m in standard form.
scheme: Move the decimal point 6 places: 5 × 10⁻⁶ m.

questions.prompt: Explain three adaptations of a sperm cell for fertilisation.
scheme: 1 · A tail allows movement towards an egg.
2 · Many mitochondria support respiration for movement.
3 · Enzymes in the head help penetrate egg coverings.

questions.prompt: Explain why most animal cells lose the ability to differentiate, while many plant cells keep it.
scheme: 1 · Most animal cells differentiate at an early stage; in adults division is mainly for repair/replacement.
2 · Plants have meristems / continue growing throughout life, so they keep producing new specialised cells.

questions.prompt: Describe how a nerve cell and a root hair cell are each adapted to their function.
scheme: 1 · Nerve cell has a long axon to carry impulses over long distances.
2 · Nerve cell has branched endings/dendrites to connect with many cells.
3 · Root hair cell has a long extension giving a large surface area.
4 · For absorbing water and mineral ions (faster) / many mitochondria for active transport.

questions.prompt: What is differentiation?
scheme: Developing specialised cell structures

questions.prompt: Why is a root hair useful?
scheme: It increases absorbing area

questions.prompt: Why does a sperm cell contain many mitochondria?
options: To store food for the embryo
To release energy for the tail to swim
scheme: Respiration in mitochondria releases energy for swimming.

questions.prompt: Why do root hair cells usually lack chloroplasts?
options: They are underground and receive no light
scheme: No light reaches roots, so chloroplasts would be no use.

questions.prompt: Which describes differentiation?
options: A cell divides into two identical cells
A cell takes in water by osmosis
A cell gains new structures to do a particular job
scheme: Differentiation is the process of a cell becoming specialised.

questions.prompt: What do the branched dendrites of a nerve cell do?
options: Connect with many other nerve cells
scheme: Branched endings let a neurone receive impulses from many cells.

questions.prompt: Describe how the cell cycle produces two genetically identical daughter cells.
scheme: 1 · DNA is replicated before division.
2 · Copies of each chromosome separate to opposite ends and nuclei divide.
3 · Cytoplasm and membrane divide, leaving identical chromosome sets.

questions.prompt: Give two ways a cell prepares for division before mitosis.
scheme: 1 · It grows / increases the number of subcellular structures such as ribosomes and mitochondria.
2 · It copies/replicates its DNA so each chromosome forms two copies.

questions.prompt: A scientist counts cells in an onion root tip: 380 cells not dividing and 20 cells in mitosis. The cell cycle takes 24 hours. Calculate the time spent in mitosis in minutes, and explain why the root tip is a good place to look.
scheme: 1 · Total cells = 400.
3 · = 72 minutes.
4 · Root tips contain meristem cells that divide frequently.

questions.prompt: Three cells each complete two rounds of division. How many result?
What happens before mitosis?
scheme: DNA is copied

questions.prompt: How many chromosomes are in a human skin cell after mitosis?
scheme: Mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same.

questions.prompt: Why must DNA be copied before mitosis?
options: So the cell can grow a cell wall
So each daughter cell receives a full set of chromosomes
scheme: Each new cell needs complete genetic information.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT a use of mitosis?
scheme: Gametes are produced by meiosis.

questions.prompt: One cell divides by mitosis five times. How many cells result?

b-stem.title: Stem cells: benefits, risks and ethics

questions.prompt: Evaluate embryonic stem cells for replacing damaged nerve tissue.
scheme: 1 · They can differentiate into a wider range of cell types than many adult stem cells.
2 · A biological risk such as infection or uncontrolled division must be considered.
3 · Potential treatment benefit must be weighed against ethical concerns about embryo use.

questions.prompt: Describe how plant meristem tissue can be used to save a rare plant species from extinction.
scheme: 1 · Meristem cells are removed from root/shoot tip.
2 · Grown on a medium/in sterile conditions to form many clones.
3 · Clones are identical, quickly produced and can be replanted/stored.

questions.prompt: Stem cells from embryos could be used to treat type 1 diabetes. Evaluate this use of stem cells.
scheme: 1 · Stem cells could be differentiated into insulin-producing pancreas cells.
2 · This could cure the condition / remove the need for insulin injections.
3 · Therapeutic cloning gives cells that are not rejected by the immune system.
4 · Risk of transferring viral infection from cultured cells.
5 · Risk of cells dividing uncontrollably / tumours.
6 · Ethical/religious objections to using embryos, with a justified conclusion.

questions.prompt: Where are adult human stem cells found?
scheme: Bone marrow

questions.prompt: Why use genetically matched stem cells?
scheme: To reduce rejection

questions.prompt: Where are meristems found in a plant?
scheme: Meristems are regions of active cell division at root and shoot tips.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of therapeutic cloning?
options: Stem cells match the patient so are not rejected
scheme: The cells have the patient's genes.

questions.prompt: Which is a risk of stem-cell treatment?
options: Cells are too large to inject
scheme: Contaminated cultures could transfer viruses.

questions.prompt: Which cell type can adult bone marrow stem cells form?
scheme: Bone marrow stem cells produce a limited range, including blood cells.

questions.prompt: Explain why alveoli exchange gases rapidly.
scheme: 1 · Many alveoli provide a large surface area.
2 · Thin walls give a short diffusion distance.
3 · Ventilation and blood flow maintain concentration gradients.

questions.prompt: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a cube of side 5 mm. Give your answer as a ratio x : 1.
scheme: 1 · Surface area = 6 × 25 = 150 mm².
2 · Volume = 125 mm³.

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of villi in the small intestine increases the rate of absorption of digested food.
scheme: 1 · Villi (and microvilli) give a large surface area.
2 · Wall is one cell thick / short diffusion distance.
3 · Rich capillary network carries absorbed molecules away.
4 · Which maintains a steep concentration gradient. Accept many mitochondria for active transport.

questions.prompt: A cube has side 2 cm. Express its surface area to volume ratio as x:1.
scheme: Area 24 cm²; volume 8 cm³; 24:8 = 3:1.

questions.prompt: Which change speeds diffusion?
scheme: A steeper gradient

questions.prompt: What is the SA:V of a 3 cm cube?
scheme: Area 54 cm², volume 27 cm³; 54 ÷ 27 = 2.

questions.prompt: How do fish gills maintain a steep concentration gradient?
options: Blood flows in the opposite direction to water
scheme: Counter-current flow keeps a gradient along the whole gill.

questions.prompt: Which change would halve the rate of diffusion across a membrane?
scheme: Rate is inversely proportional to the diffusion distance.

questions.prompt: Why do single-celled organisms not need a gas exchange system?
options: They have a large surface area to volume ratio
They are too small to need oxygen
scheme: Diffusion across the membrane meets their needs.

questions.prompt: Explain why potato tissue loses mass in concentrated sugar solution.
scheme: 1 · The outside solution is more concentrated than the cell contents.
2 · Water moves out by osmosis across partially permeable cell membranes.
3 · Water loss reduces tissue mass.

questions.prompt: Explain why potato cylinders should be blotted dry before reweighing.
scheme: 1 · Removes surface solution/water.
2 · So the mass measured is only that of the tissue / measurements are comparable.

questions.prompt: Describe a method to find the concentration of sucrose solution with the same water concentration as potato cells.
scheme: 1 · Cut potato cylinders of the same size/with the same borer and length.
2 · Blot and weigh each cylinder.
3 · Place in a range of sucrose concentrations, e.g. 0 to 1.0 mol/dm³.
4 · Leave for the same time at the same temperature.
5 · Remove, blot dry in the same way and reweigh; calculate percentage change.
6 · Plot % change against concentration; where the line crosses zero is the answer.

questions.prompt: A cylinder changes from 4.0 g to 3.6 g. Calculate percentage mass change.
When does water enter a cell by osmosis?
options: Outside is more dilute than inside
scheme: Outside is more dilute than inside

questions.prompt: A potato piece goes from 2.50 g to 2.00 g. What is the percentage change?
Why might a red blood cell burst in pure water?
options: It gains water by osmosis and has no cell wall
scheme: Animal cells have no wall to resist swelling.

questions.prompt: Why is percentage change in mass calculated rather than change in mass?
options: It removes the need for repeats
The pieces had different starting masses
scheme: Percentages allow fair comparison.

questions.prompt: What describes a plant cell that has lost a lot of water?
scheme: Cells that lose water become flaccid.

questions.prompt: Explain why low oxygen availability can reduce mineral uptake by roots.
scheme: 1 · Less oxygen reduces aerobic respiration.
2 · Less energy is available for active transport.
3 · Mineral ions need to move against their concentration gradient.

questions.prompt: Give two differences between diffusion and active transport.
scheme: 1 · Diffusion is down a concentration gradient; active transport is against it.
2 · Diffusion is passive/needs no energy; active transport needs energy from respiration. Accept active transport uses carrier proteins.

questions.prompt: Waterlogged soil contains little oxygen. Explain why plants in waterlogged soil may show signs of mineral deficiency.
scheme: 1 · Root cells receive less oxygen.
2 · So less aerobic respiration / less energy released.
3 · Active transport of mineral ions needs energy.
4 · So fewer mineral ions (e.g. nitrate/magnesium) are absorbed against the gradient.

questions.prompt: Which process requires energy from respiration?
scheme: Active transport

questions.prompt: Mineral concentration is lower in soil than a root cell. Uptake uses…
scheme: Active transport

questions.prompt: What do carrier proteins do in active transport?
options: Move particles across the membrane using energy
scheme: Carrier proteins transport substances against the gradient.

questions.prompt: Why do plants need nitrate ions?
scheme: Nitrate supplies nitrogen for amino acids and proteins.

questions.prompt: Glucose is absorbed from the gut when its concentration in the gut is lower than in the blood. This uses…
scheme: Movement against the gradient requires active transport.

questions.prompt: Which process involves water moving through a partially permeable membrane?
scheme: Osmosis is specific to water.

questions.prompt: Explain three precautions in preparing a bacterial culture.
scheme: 1 · Sterilise medium and equipment to remove contaminants.
2 · Minimise lid opening to reduce airborne contamination.
3 · Secure without fully sealing the lid and incubate at 25°C to reduce risk.

questions.prompt: A culture starts with 500 bacteria. The mean division time is 25 minutes. Calculate the number of bacteria after 150 minutes. Give your answer in standard form.
scheme: 1 · Number of divisions = 150 ÷ 25 = 6.

questions.prompt: Describe how to investigate the effect of three different antiseptics on the growth of bacteria.
scheme: 1 · Use sterile agar plate and spread bacteria evenly with sterile technique.
2 · Soak paper discs of the same size in each antiseptic.
3 · Include a control disc soaked in sterile water.
4 · Place discs on the agar, tape lid and incubate at 25 °C.
5 · Measure the diameter of each clear zone after a set time.
6 · Calculate area with πr² and compare; repeat for reliable means.

questions.prompt: A clear circle has diameter 10 mm. Use π = 3.14 to calculate area.
scheme: Radius 5 mm; 3.14 × 25 = 78.5 mm².

questions.prompt: Why incubate school cultures at 25°C?
scheme: To reduce harmful-pathogen risk

questions.prompt: Why is the inoculating loop passed through a flame?
scheme: Flaming sterilises the loop.

questions.prompt: Why is the Petri dish lid taped but not sealed all round?
options: So oxygen can enter and anaerobic pathogens are not encouraged
scheme: Taping lets air in and prevents harmful anaerobic growth.

questions.prompt: A bacterium divides every 20 minutes. How many bacteria are produced from one after 2 hours?
scheme: 2 hours = 6 divisions; 2⁶ = 64.

questions.prompt: How do bacteria reproduce?
scheme: Bacteria divide by binary fission.

b-review-cells.title: Cell biology: review and exam practice

questions.prompt: A student views onion cells. Describe how to prepare the slide and focus on the cells.
scheme: 1 · Peel thin layer of onion epidermis and place on slide in a drop of water/iodine.
2 · Lower coverslip at an angle to avoid air bubbles.
3 · Start with the lowest-power objective.
4 · Use coarse focus then fine focus to get a clear image.

questions.prompt: A cell measures 0.05 mm. A student's drawing of the cell is 25 mm long. Calculate the magnification.
Compare diffusion, osmosis and active transport.
scheme: 1 · Diffusion: net movement of particles from high to low concentration.
2 · Diffusion is passive / needs no energy.
3 · Osmosis: movement of water through a partially permeable membrane.
4 · From dilute to concentrated solution, passive.
5 · Active transport moves substances against a gradient.
6 · Needs energy from respiration / uses carrier proteins, e.g. mineral uptake by roots.

questions.prompt: Explain why a multicellular organism needs exchange surfaces and a transport system.
scheme: 1 · Large organisms have a small SA:V.
2 · Diffusion alone is too slow over long distances to supply all cells.
3 · Exchange surfaces increase area; transport system carries substances to cells.

questions.prompt: Which structure controls what enters and leaves a cell?
scheme: The membrane is partially permeable.

questions.prompt: An image is 4.8 mm long at × 400. What is the real length?
Which cell type is specialised to carry impulses?
scheme: Nerve cells have long axons.

questions.prompt: What is the main function of mitosis in adults?
scheme: Mitosis gives identical cells.

questions.prompt: Stem cells from embryos can…
scheme: Embryonic stem cells are very versatile.

questions.prompt: Which process moves glucose from a low concentration in the gut into the blood?
scheme: Against a gradient requires energy.

questions.prompt: A cube of side 4 cm has SA:V of…
A potato piece changes from 5.0 g to 5.6 g. Percentage change?
Why do electron microscopes show more detail?
scheme: Resolution determines detail.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT found in a bacterial cell?
scheme: Prokaryotes lack mitochondria.

questions.prompt: Explain how bile assists fat digestion.
scheme: 1 · It neutralises acid, providing alkaline conditions for lipase.
2 · It emulsifies fat into smaller droplets.
3 · This increases surface area available to lipase.

questions.prompt: Give the level of organisation of the stomach and explain your answer.
scheme: 1 · Organ.
2 · It is made of several tissues (e.g. muscle, glandular, epithelial) working together for a function.

questions.prompt: Describe how a protein in food is digested and how the products are used in the body.
scheme: 1 · Protease/pepsin in the stomach begins breaking protein down.
2 · Proteases from the pancreas/small intestine complete digestion to amino acids.
3 · Amino acids are absorbed into the blood through the villi/small intestine wall.
4 · Amino acids are used to build new proteins (e.g. enzymes, muscle).

questions.prompt: Protein digestion produces…
scheme: Amino acids

questions.prompt: Where is bile made?
scheme: Liver

questions.prompt: Which organ produces lipase, protease and amylase?
scheme: The pancreas secretes all three.

questions.prompt: Why does the stomach contain hydrochloric acid?
options: To kill microorganisms and give the low pH for pepsin
scheme: Acid kills pathogens and suits stomach protease.

questions.prompt: What are the products of lipid digestion?
scheme: Lipase breaks lipids into fatty acids and glycerol.

questions.prompt: Where is most water absorbed?
scheme: The large intestine absorbs water from undigested material.

questions.prompt: Explain why an enzyme works well at 37°C but poorly at 70°C.
scheme: 1 · High temperature alters protein structure.
2 · The active site changes shape / denatures.
3 · Fewer substrate molecules fit, so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form.

questions.prompt: Explain why a protease does not digest starch.
scheme: 1 · The active site has a specific shape.
2 · Starch is not complementary to/does not fit the protease active site.

questions.prompt: Describe how to investigate the effect of pH on the rate of starch digestion by amylase.
scheme: 1 · Add iodine drops to each well of a spotting tile.
2 · Mix amylase, starch and a buffer of known pH in a test tube.
3 · Keep at constant temperature in a water bath.
4 · Every 30 s transfer a drop to iodine; record time until iodine stays orange-brown.
5 · Repeat with buffers of different pH (e.g. 5, 6, 7, 8).
6 · Keep volumes/concentrations of starch and amylase the same; repeat and calculate rate = 1/time.

questions.prompt: Starch digestion takes 25 s. Calculate 1/time.
Why is a denatured enzyme less effective?
options: Its active site no longer fits the substrate
scheme: Its active site no longer fits the substrate

questions.prompt: What happens to an enzyme's active site when it denatures?
options: It gets bigger and works faster
It changes shape so the substrate no longer fits
scheme: Denaturing alters the active site shape.

questions.prompt: Starch was all digested after 120 s. What is the relative rate as 1000/time?
In the amylase practical, what does a blue-black colour with iodine show?
scheme: Iodine turns blue-black with starch.

questions.prompt: Why are buffer solutions used in the pH practical?
scheme: Buffers resist pH change.

questions.prompt: A food turns iodine blue-black but heated Benedict’s stays blue. Interpret the results and name a useful control.
scheme: 1 · Starch is detected.
2 · Reducing sugar is not detected under the conditions.
3 · A known sugar solution checks the Benedict’s reagent and heating.

questions.prompt: Name a hazard in the Biuret test and how to reduce the risk.
scheme: 1 · Biuret/sodium hydroxide/copper sulfate is an irritant/corrosive.
2 · Wear eye protection / wash spills from skin immediately.

questions.prompt: Describe how a student could compare the amount of reducing sugar in three fruit juices.
scheme: 1 · Add the same volume of each juice to separate tubes with the same volume of Benedict's.
2 · Heat in a water bath (~75 °C) for the same time.
3 · Compare colours: blue/green/yellow/brick-red.
4 · Use standards of known glucose concentration / a colorimeter to estimate concentration.

questions.prompt: Which indicates protein?
scheme: Lilac Biuret result

questions.prompt: Which test requires a hot water bath?
scheme: Benedict’s

questions.prompt: What is the positive result for the Biuret test?
scheme: Biuret turns lilac with protein.

questions.prompt: Which test must be heated?
scheme: Benedict's is heated in a water bath.

questions.prompt: Which Benedict's colour shows the most reducing sugar?
scheme: Red indicates the highest concentration.

questions.prompt: Why is the food ground and filtered before testing?
options: To make a clear solution of the food
scheme: A clear solution makes colour changes visible.

questions.prompt: Explain why the left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall than the right.
scheme: 1 · It pumps blood around the whole body.
2 · It must generate a higher pressure.
3 · More muscle produces a greater force of contraction.

questions.prompt: Describe the function of the coronary arteries.
scheme: 1 · Supply blood to the heart muscle.
2 · Bringing oxygen/glucose for respiration/contraction.

questions.prompt: Describe the pathway of blood from the vena cava to the aorta, naming the structures it passes through.
scheme: 1 · Vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle.
2 · Pulmonary artery to the lungs, where blood is oxygenated.
3 · Pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle.
4 · Valves prevent backflow; blood leaves through the aorta.

questions.prompt: Which vessel carries blood to lungs?
scheme: Pulmonary artery

questions.prompt: 70 cm³ per beat at 80 beats/min gives what flow?
Which chamber pumps blood into the aorta?
scheme: The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood to the body.

questions.prompt: Why do veins have valves?
options: To prevent backflow of low-pressure blood
scheme: Valves keep blood moving towards the heart.

questions.prompt: Why are capillary walls one cell thick?
options: To give a short diffusion distance
scheme: Thin walls allow rapid exchange.

questions.prompt: Stroke volume 70 cm³, heart rate 72 beats/min. Cardiac output is…
Give a benefit and limitation of a stent and explain why coronary flow matters.
scheme: 1 · A stent improves blood flow through a narrowed artery.
2 · Surgery, infection or clotting presents a risk.
3 · Heart muscle receives more oxygen for aerobic respiration.

questions.prompt: Explain two ways red blood cells are adapted to carry oxygen.
scheme: 1 · Biconcave shape gives large surface area for diffusion.
2 · No nucleus so more space for haemoglobin / contains haemoglobin that binds oxygen.

questions.prompt: Coronary heart disease can be treated with stents, statins or a heart transplant. Evaluate these treatments.
scheme: 1 · Stent opens the narrowed artery and restores blood flow quickly.
2 · Stent surgery has risks, e.g. clots, infection, artery may narrow again.
3 · Statins reduce cholesterol and slow fatty deposit build-up.
4 · Statins must be taken long-term and may have side effects / take time to work.
5 · Transplant needed for heart failure but requires a donor and immunosuppressants.
6 · A justified conclusion linked to severity/situation.

questions.prompt: Which component helps clot blood?
scheme: Platelets

questions.prompt: What does a coronary stent do?
scheme: Keeps a narrowed artery open

questions.prompt: Why do red blood cells have no nucleus?
scheme: This lets them carry more oxygen.

questions.prompt: What do statins do?
scheme: Statins lower LDL cholesterol.

questions.prompt: Which part of blood transports urea?
scheme: Urea is dissolved in plasma.

questions.prompt: A disadvantage of mechanical valves is that…
options: they wear out in a few years
patients need drugs to prevent blood clots
scheme: Mechanical valves increase clot risk.

questions.prompt: Why does a survey linking low exercise and heart disease not prove causation?
scheme: 1 · Correlation alone does not establish cause.
2 · A confounding factor such as age or smoking may affect both.
3 · Further evidence with appropriate comparisons / controls is needed.

questions.prompt: Explain why malignant tumours are more dangerous than benign tumours.
scheme: 1 · Malignant cells invade neighbouring tissues.
2 · They spread in the blood to form secondary tumours elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Discuss how lifestyle factors can affect the risk of non-communicable diseases. Give examples.
scheme: 1 · Smoking increases risk of lung cancer / lung and cardiovascular disease.
2 · Poor diet/obesity increases risk of type 2 diabetes / cardiovascular disease.
3 · Excess alcohol damages the liver / brain.
4 · Risk factors increase probability, not certainty; several factors may interact.

questions.prompt: A risk factor…
scheme: Increases disease probability

questions.prompt: A malignant tumour can…
scheme: Invade tissues and spread

questions.prompt: Which is a non-communicable disease?
scheme: Type 2 diabetes is not passed between people.

questions.prompt: What is a carcinogen?
options: Something that increases the risk of cancer
scheme: Carcinogens, such as tar, increase cancer risk.

questions.prompt: Benign tumours…
options: stay in one place in a membrane
scheme: Benign tumours do not invade other tissues.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of diseases interacting?
scheme: Some viruses can trigger cancer.

questions.prompt: Explain why wind can increase water uptake by a leafy shoot.
scheme: 1 · Wind removes humid air near the leaf.
2 · The steeper gradient increases water-vapour diffusion / transpiration.
3 · Water lost from leaves is replaced through the xylem.

questions.prompt: Explain why most stomata are found on the lower surface of a leaf.
scheme: 1 · The lower surface is cooler/shaded.
2 · So less water is lost by evaporation/transpiration.

questions.prompt: Describe how a potometer could be used to investigate the effect of air movement on the rate of water uptake.
scheme: 1 · Cut shoot under water and fit to potometer under water / seal airtight.
2 · Introduce an air bubble and record distance moved in a set time.
3 · Use a fan at different distances/speeds to change air movement.
4 · Keep light intensity, temperature and the same shoot constant.
5 · Repeat readings and calculate a mean.
6 · Calculate rate = distance (or volume) ÷ time and compare.

questions.prompt: Which tissue transports sugars?
scheme: Phloem

questions.prompt: Why does high humidity reduce transpiration?
scheme: It reduces the water-vapour gradient

questions.prompt: What happens to stomata when guard cells lose water?
scheme: Flaccid guard cells close the stoma.

questions.prompt: Which tissue contains the most chloroplasts?
scheme: Palisade cells are packed with chloroplasts.

questions.prompt: Translocation is the movement of…
scheme: Phloem moves sugars from sources to sinks.

questions.prompt: Why are xylem walls strengthened with lignin?
options: To support the plant and withstand water pressure
scheme: Lignin makes hollow tubes strong.

questions.prompt: Describe how to test a food sample for protein and for starch.
scheme: 1 · Grind food with water and filter.
2 · Add Biuret reagent; lilac/purple shows protein.
3 · Add iodine solution.
4 · Blue-black shows starch.

questions.prompt: Stroke volume is 80 cm³ and heart rate is 75 beats per minute. Calculate cardiac output in dm³/min.
scheme: 2 · = 6.0 dm³/min.

questions.prompt: Explain how the structures of arteries, veins and capillaries are related to their functions.
scheme: 1 · Arteries have thick muscular walls to withstand high pressure.
2 · Elastic fibres stretch and recoil / narrow lumen.
3 · Veins have thin walls and a wide lumen as pressure is low.
4 · Veins have valves to prevent backflow.
5 · Capillaries have walls one cell thick.
6 · Short diffusion distance for exchange with tissues.

questions.prompt: Explain why a high level of saturated fat in the diet increases the risk of a heart attack.
scheme: 1 · Increases blood cholesterol / fatty deposits in coronary arteries.
2 · Arteries narrow so less blood flows to heart muscle.
3 · Less oxygen reaches heart muscle, so cells die / heart attack.

questions.prompt: Which enzyme digests protein?
scheme: Proteases break proteins into amino acids.

questions.prompt: Which vessel carries oxygenated blood from the lungs?
scheme: The pulmonary vein returns blood to the heart.

questions.prompt: Which food test needs heating?
scheme: Benedict's test requires a water bath.

questions.prompt: A risk factor for type 2 diabetes is…
scheme: Obesity raises the risk.

questions.prompt: What do platelets do?
scheme: Platelets help form clots.

questions.prompt: Where are stomata mostly found?
scheme: The lower surface is cooler.

questions.prompt: Which factor increases transpiration?
scheme: Warmer air increases evaporation.

questions.prompt: At 70 °C an enzyme stops working because…
options: its active site has changed shape
scheme: High temperature denatures it.

questions.prompt: Which tissue carries water up a plant?
scheme: Xylem carries water and minerals.

questions.prompt: A stent is used to…
scheme: Stents hold arteries open.

questions.prompt: Explain how mosquito nets and removing standing water reduce malaria spread.
scheme: 1 · Nets reduce mosquito bites.
2 · Removing standing water reduces mosquito breeding.
3 · Fewer bites by infected mosquitoes reduce protist transmission.

questions.prompt: Describe the symptoms of HIV and how it is controlled.
scheme: 1 · Initial flu-like symptoms.
2 · Virus attacks immune cells; late stage AIDS when immune system badly damaged.
3 · Controlled with antiretroviral drugs.

questions.prompt: Compare how measles, Salmonella and rose black spot are spread, and suggest one way to reduce the spread of each.
scheme: 1 · Measles spread by droplets / inhalation.
2 · Reduced by vaccination / isolating infected people.
3 · Salmonella spread in food / undercooked food / unhygienic preparation.
4 · Reduced by vaccinating poultry / cooking thoroughly / hygiene.
5 · Rose black spot spread by spores in wind/water.
6 · Reduced by removing/burning infected leaves / fungicides.

questions.prompt: What causes malaria?
options: The mosquito itself as a bacterium
scheme: A protist

questions.prompt: Why can TMV reduce growth?
scheme: Leaf damage reduces photosynthesis

questions.prompt: Which disease is caused by a fungus?
scheme: Rose black spot is a fungal disease.

questions.prompt: How is measles spread?
options: Inhalation of droplets from sneezes and coughs
scheme: Measles is airborne in droplets.

questions.prompt: Why do viruses damage cells?
options: They reproduce inside cells and burst them
scheme: New viruses are released when cells burst.

questions.prompt: A vector is…
options: an organism that carries a pathogen between hosts
scheme: The mosquito is a vector for malaria.
